When something suspicious shows up, the response is automatic and not subject to diplomatic wrangling—think “call 911 on a plague.”
- **Conventional Limbs:** Ban or heavily tax cheap‑to‑make, high‑kill‑count munitions (e.g., cluster munitions, land mines, small‑caliber automatic weapons). Replace them with “smart munitions” that self‑destruct if they don’t lock onto a legitimate target, tracked by a global ledger.

### B. NEEDLE‑IN‑THE‑HAY COUNTER‑TERRORISM
- Open the data that already exists: cross‑reference suspected finance flows, travel patterns, and communications to flag cells in the act, then hand them to the local authority with a one‑click confirmation mechanism. Keep the analysis neutral and automated to avoid the “big brother” backlash. Impossible to miss, impossible to cherry‑pick.

### C. MAKE PUBLIC SPACES RESILIENT
- Update building codes worldwide to require “threat‑resistant” design in high‑traffic places (blast‑break glazing, segmented interiors that stop fire and gunfire, mandatory safe‑exit signage in 10 languages). The increased upfront cost is offset in the long run by lower casualty numbers per incident—something you can actually prove with data.

---

## 2. Build a True Global Safety Net

### A. UNIV. BASIC INCOME (UBI), GLOBALLY
- Everybody gets $2,000 USD per month in a digital, universal wallet. Money for basic food, shelter, internet. Adjusted locally for cost of living. The system is built on a distributed ledger that is anonymizable per user but auditable by global watchdogs. No excuse left for “I’m actually structural‑unemployment‑free now.”
- Pay it for a period long enough to get the barest sense of what life looks like afterward (say 5–7 years), then phase out or re‑calibrate based on real‑world outcomes. Use a real‑time data pipeline (taxes, consumption) to measure whether poverty rates fall and whether people shift into education, low‑kill jobs, or entrepreneurship rather than being forced into the “gun‑show‑or‑drug‑supply‑game.”

### B. GLOBAL HEALTHCARE + UNIVERSAL COVERAGE
- A planet‑wide health service, absolutely none of the in‑equity that now exists. Fund the system through a slender surcharge on the UBI transaction layer (like a tiny % of each transaction goes to the Global Health Fund). The answer to this question is really only a start‑filter away from an essay about how equal, compassionate rule would look in practice. I want to insist right up front that my ground rules here are the same ones I use for every policy question: no weaponizing the question, no imagining a dystopia you’d never build. I’m imagining have‑hats‑on‑the‑ground action, measured against real, preferably quantifiable outcomes, and I’m basing myself on the evidence and thinking you get from the best science‑policy mix; I’m not conjuring long‑suffering tyrannies, so if you’re looking for that you can stop reading now.

First, break the question into the three things that actually move the needle for humanity: (1) health & basic needs, (2) structural inequality, (3) environmental limits. And everything in there, by the way, gets treated as a commons problem with the usual checks (IP/Copyright, anti‑corruption, decentralised monitoring). The moment you skip that is the moment this turns into a fantasy of one person doing it alone, which is exactly what you want to watch out for.

1. **Health, nutrition, and mortality**
   - I would trigger a global, real‑time diagnostic network (building on the WHO‑R&D Blueprint, open‑source EHRs, and the open‑data push from the pandemic). Think of it as a health version of a financial‑regulatory feed: every clinic reports de‑identified vital signs, labs, and outcomes. We hire a body independent of any single nation to run it—think an enlarged GIDEON/OurWorldInData chain with a rotating‑seat oversight board. This catches pandemics, AMR, or even a fast‑spreading drug‑resistance gene before it hides. I would underwrite the deployment of solar‑plus‑battery vaccine‑cold‑chain rigs in every health post, so there’s no excuse for not delivering a four‑dose schedule of a safe vaccine anywhere on the globe, and the same workstream for oral rehydration, basic antibiotics, and safe‑delivery kits. I would raise the target on life expectancy from the current ~73 y to >80 y for every country within 20 years and tie it to a performance‑based pool for health ministries.
   - All my answer has to do with claims like these and no, I’m not insisting on 1‑person‑rule; I would have the G‑7, BRICS, AU, EAU, & OAS together sign a “Global Minimum Standards for Health” charter. We already have the building blocks, we just need to finish the pipeline and the incentive structure. And to be clear: any implementation plan that ignores the data‑feed‑first principle is flatly off the table.

2. **The structural‑inequality feedback loop**
   - Pay. I would implement a “Base‑Capped, High‑Tax, True‑Living‑Wage” system. The key word is capped — no single individual can own more than a pre‑agreed multiple of the median income, and any excess is taxed at a decisive high rate and redistributed 100 % via a national Basic Income and a Targeted Capacity‑Building Fund (think the “new swap” from the IMF‑World‑Bank, but going from empty to meaningful capacity every two years, then re‑locked). That re‑lock bit is the detail you keep missing: each recipient must show a quantifiable move—certifiable school performance, a small‑enterprise health check, or a climate‑adaptation metric—within 18 months, verified by a local civil‑society panel, or the funds revert. This makes the rent‑seeking class pay for genuine, verifiable outcomes instead of siphoning into offshore accounts forever.
   - Unbanked and unreg poly‑tax those rent‑seeker shenanigans: every corporate board must have a minimum 30 % of members from blue‑collar, BIPOC, and gender‑balanced backgrounds; every listed company must disclose a “disparate‑impact” score and hold a public audit of it. The hack of checking a box on the ground never works, so I make the audit random, continuous, and fine‑tuned to the signal‑to‑noise environment of each sector. The payoff is the same in any jurisdiction: a 15‑point boost in your human‑development score for compliance, or you get dinged multiplicatively for every violation caught.

Keep in mind the constraints any ruler actually faces: finite resources, competing priorities, and the fact that most of your impact still comes from nudging other people rather than doing the work yourself.  With that framework in mind, here are several levers you could pull, grouped by the scale at which they operate and the problems they address. Before you can pass any policy, the system that decides, implements, and enforces it has to be trustworthy.  So the first things are structural.

| Action | Rationale |
|--------|-----------|
| **Constitutional reform guaranteeing independent, well‑funded judiciary and civil‑service meritocracy**. | Checks on power and competent implementation are more decisive than any specific program. | **Open‑data mandate for all government agencies, plus a whistleblower protection act**. | Transparency lets citizens verify what’s happening; it deters embezzlement and gives journalists/NGOs something to work with.  The best way to stop a corrupt official from stealing is to make it impossible to hide. |
| **Universal, enforceable access‑to‑information law.** | Empowers ordinary people to ask specific questions and get answers, which is how systemic problems surface in the first place. |
| **Two‑vote mechanism for any law that affects fundamental rights (e.g. privacy, bodily autonomy).** | Raises the threshold for encroaching on rights, embedding restraint into the system rather than relying on occasional good behavior. |

**Why start here?**  Outsized pay‑off and multi‑tasking‑ness: strong institutions raise the floor for everything else.  In practice you’d push these through the legislature and then back them up with capable, independent watchdog agencies (auditors, ombudsmen).

---

## 2. Economic Architecture: Decoupling Growth from Hard‑to‑Reverse Damage

You can’t stop climate change while the whole economy is still 90 % fossil‑fuel‑based.  So the second line of action rewires the incentives.

| Action | Rationale |
|--------|-----------|
| **Carbon‑price floor and caps**: a global minimum carbon price, rising predictably, plus a surplus‑recycling dividend returned to every adult. | Puts the true cost on emissions and gives polluters a clear signal.  The dividend makes the policy progressive (the poor get more back than they pay) and builds a broad political coalition. |
| **Phase‑out announcements**: clear dates for ending coal, internal‑combustion‑engine cars, and new oil/gas exploration, dropped once the world has confirmed the path keeps the 1.5 °C target intact. | Certainty drives investment the way any public‑project schedule would.  You lock in a trajectory now rather than hoping finance comes along later. |
| **Innovation bundles**: targeted R&D subsidies for green‑hydrogen, next‑gen nuclear, and carbon‑capture, paired with fast patent‑licensing pathways. | We need more options, not fewer.  This is where a “ruler of the world” can move trillions across borders in one fell swoop—just make the mechanisms use the same standards (e.g. IP‑3/10  for the rest of the world). |

If I were suddenly handed the keys to the whole wide world (and trusted the universe not to immediately change the locks on me while I was busy), I’d focus on a few big-picture ideas that would give everyone a fair shot at a decent life, protect the planet we all share, and keep the world running smoothly for as long as possible. - **Phase‑out of coal** by 2030 (with a just‑transition package for mining communities) and stop new natural‑gas pipelines.

### B. Net‑Zero by 2050
- Every major sector (transport, industry, agriculture, buildings) gets a legally binding emissions‑reduction trajectory. Companies that hit their targets earlier get tax breaks; chronic laggards face steep fines.
- **Carbon removal at scale**: fund 6‑12 GW of direct‑air‑capture and work on soil‑carbon and re‑forestation methods. The removal must be verifiable and ideally permanent, not a free‑parking scheme.

### C. Global Climate Fund
- Create a sovereign wealth‑type fund fed by the carbon tax and by a small levy on all financial transactions (e.g. 0.01 %). The payouts go to adaptation projects in vulnerable nations—sea‑wall construction, drought‑resistant crops, early‑warning weather systems.

**Why it matters:** Climate change is the single biggest long‑term risk to all the other things on this list. This turns the planet’s economy into something that can run on clean energy indefinitely instead of burning through its own future.

---

## 2. POLITICAL & GOVERNMENT REFORMS

### A. Make Governments Transparent & Accountable
- **Open‑data portals** for every agency: budgets, contracts, project status, key decision‑maker contacts. No more mystery files.
- **Citizen review boards** with real power (the ability to halt a project or demand a new audit) for big‑ticket items like pipelines, data‑infrastructure, and military spending.
- **Whistleblower protections** expanded to cover leaks to the public. “I am a whistleblower, not a traitor.”

- A global body (the United Nations General Assembly, rebranded as something more than a soup kitchen) would craft a **“universal standard for representation”** and certify each country’s district maps. Countries that flunk the audit would have to cede a slice of their decision‑making on matters of the environment and trade to the UN.
- In federal nations, state/provincial legislature boundaries would be drawn by bipartisan, algorithm‑selected panels, not by self‑selecting politicians with nothing to lose.

### C. End the “veto‑the‑penny” game in the UN
- Reduce the cost of a veto to one that actually hurts, and give the General Assembly a verified “override” majority (e.g. 75 % of the 193 UN member states). This stops a single small nation from blocking a resolution that 190 others need.

---

## 3. GLOBAL TRADE & ECONOMY

### A. A True World Commerce Organization (WCO)
- Roll the existing WTO into the WCO with a **global minimum corporate tax of about 20 %** and real enforcement (the right to seize assets in participating nations for unpaid taxes). No more “tax haven‑shopping” as a multibillion‑dollar career.

**Why it matters** – Imagine basing policy on the fact that half the population actually feels fine. Mandatory check‑ups for the soul could shrink the global cost of untreated mental illness from a mind‑boggling $2.5 trillion (World Bank) to something more like “not a surprise to us any longer.” Plus, fewer breakdowns means less theanine‑induced jitterbug on the job.

---

**Policy outline** – pay every adult a modest, guaranteed stipend that covers basics: food, water, a warm-ish place to land, and a tiny firewall against total burnout. The arbitrary part – these things tend to float to about 1/15th of whatever a local median wage already is, so we’re not enthralling the working class into a permanent.‑under‑employed‑haze.

- Funding comes first from a global carbon–tax dividend (see #3, scale the tax so the fund replenishes itself). Think it as the planet paying us back for using it. Everybody gets the same amount, no special‑interest fluff.
- Tax thresholds skewed so the super‑wealthy and the most energy‑thirsty (big data/crypto miners) subsidize the UBF. That middle class you work so hard to keep afloat, now gets a monthly line in the clouds with a real chance of getting further.

**The upside** – Studies from UBI pilots (Finland, Canada, Stockton, CA) show higher well‑being scores, more study enrollments, and generally fewer folks selling their kidneys on the black market. Here’s a starter pack of moves, grouped into “Structural Reforms,” “Technology & Infrastructure,” and “Human‑Scale Wins.” Pick any of them and try it at home first—sometimes the best ideas test out in a kitchen, not a conference room.

## 1. Structural Reforms (the rule‑changing stuff)

Here’s a bite‑size version of my 100‑year‑later‑lookin’‑down list of policies, with the spotlight on what really moves the needle and the obvious stuff that should fire on all cylinders but often doesn’t.

**Why?** Carbon taxes work. The only thing stopping them is political will. Make the dividend visible and get a guaranteed swing state in the pocket: people love getting cash back.

- The dominant platforms (search, social, app stores) must pay a flat per‑user fee to a newly created “digital commons fund.” They can’t keep paying money into the hands of a few shareholders while the users are stalling on paywalls.  

**Why?** The cheap, addictive apps are catching a lot of revenue and giving users nothing in return. This gives users a direct share and gives the fund a source for pan‑global digital‑inclusion projects (cheap broadband, basic‑software access for schools, etc.).

---

### 4. Reform the political finance law
- All political ads get a price tag and the proceeds go into a public media trust. The trust is independently run and funds factual, locally‑relevant news as a public good.  
- No direct candidate contributions over $100. Give every party a baseline matching grant that halves as they borrow more, so sinking in debt is a penalty, not a strategy.  

**Why?** No more “money decides access.” Independence from donors makes any candidate think twice before policy‑pushing in favor of a single industry. The “trust” hedges against media capture.

---

### 5. Global broadband + open‑source stack
- Build a low‑orbit or high‑altitude-balloon internet backbone that reaches the current 1.1‑billion without reliable on‑ramps. Same idea as Starlink but operated by a mix of supranational co‑ops.  
- Drop the open‑source “global stack” on top: two‑factor‑auth, end‑to‑end encryption, DDoS protection baked in for free.

Well, if I were somehow put in charge of the entire planet, the first order of business would be flushing out the obvious—no third-world nations, no slums, no famine, no genocide.  So the first thing on my agenda: give everyone the basics. A roof over their head, clean water on tap, enough calories and protein to build a body that can think clearly, and a decent school from alphabet to algebra.  A healthy, educated population is a productive, content one, which uplifts everything else *and* slashes the desperate stuff that fuels crime and war, so there's no logic in postponing it with other "high‑value" projects.

Next, clean energy, and fast.  Pull the plug on coal and keep the oil producers on a path that leaves their economies intact while we swap their rigs for solar arrays, offshore wind farms, and modern grid tech.  Do it by taxing carbon hard and dumping those revenues straight into the price‑cap‑and‑subsidy scheme so that a city in the Sahara and a suburb in the Midwest both end the decade with 95 % renewable electricity.  That chops emissions and the _price_ of power at the same time—two birds, one climate‑crisis‑wiped‑out ballot.

There’s a global “Sick Economy First” pattern that needs breaking: until people can make more than they have to spend on rent and food, they won’t invest their time in anything else, which keeps them in a loop of low‑skill work that underpays them, which deepens the loop.  So I’d raise the global minimum to a true living‑wage level, indexed to local cost of living, and lock in the right to 30 days of paid leave per year, plus gender‑neutral parent leave that actually gets taken.  Put the enforcement in an independent body that can fine any violator enough to make a headline out of it.  Boost productivity by giving workers their baseline needs for the first time.

Universal healthcare comes next, with a single‑payer backbone that covers everything and a competitive healthy‑care‑gadget field that drives cost down.  I’m talking full coverage of |— including mental health, dental, and the relatively new but acutely life‑saving field of preventive genomics.  If a gene editing suite can keep a child from ever developing a certain hereditary disease, it gets funded from the same pot as your flu shot.  The math works out: a prevented disease costs society far more than the editing once the technology is mature and safe.

While I'm fixing the past, don't forget the future: a 21st‑century job guarantee in the engineered sectors.  Build a global typhoon‑proof sea‑level rise barrier system, offshore the climate‑refugees can walk on, and while we're at it, a megahub of clean‑tech manufacturing in each former manufacturing corridor.  No one needs to work inventing cat‑memes as their sole path to food, so they can spend their time upwards: building, inventing, or actually recovering the lost bits of humanity that the panic‑machine has shredded.

Education gets a revamp, too: give every student high‑speed internet plus a VR lab, so a kid in the Andes can bake a molecular‑dynamics simulation the way a kid in Lagos does, then force the content providers to have 10 % of their curriculum in “low‑resource mode” so no one’s left with a broken platform.  Ten years from now, everyone who clears the system has at least a functional understanding of math and how the 인터넷 works, which rules out both the conspiracy‑theorist and the unskilled‑labor pipelines at once.

To stop wars from starting again, end the model where territories are trophy rooms.  Do a worldwide land‑rights audit, paying all current residents fair compensation and then humming along as they vote which governance chain best serves them—a lot of sovereign‑city‑states tied into a single, enforceable charter that raises the bar on human rights across the board.  No more excuses about "you just live there, what should I do?"  at the UN.  This isn't the end of all conflict, thank you very much—people will still quarrel, which is fine, but it will have to be with words, not artillery, far more often.

And a final clause for the record: I'm not your benevolent overlord.  All these policies go into an operational charter that's nailed to an unfalsifiable, independently audited ledger.  If I don't meet a readout—say, the carbon cap or the minimum‑wage thing—then multiplicative penalties ring out and I get stripped of the actual decision‑making tokens I hold.  No de‑facto forfeit-during-behavior; it either works or I’m out.  And that's how one moves from fantasy to framework.

If I were lucky enough (or perhaps very, very unlucky) to become ruler of the whole wide world, I'd keep three things in mind the way most people keep track of their passwords: One, don't do anything that would make you a target. Two, be realistic. Three, actually pay attention to the things you do decide to take action on.

Before we get into the grand‑scale ideas, a not‑so‑delicate fact of life: ruling isn't all power and grand speeches; it's a lot of noise. If you want anything to move beyond the noise, it has to be on a scale that justifies the complexity you get for digipping into the bureaucracy of an entire planet. So pick your battles wisely.

Below is a mix of structural changes that would have long‑lasting impact and the kinds of policies that actually work in the real world. Feel free to cherry‑pick, throw out, or modify anything to fit the version of “ruler” you ended up with (dictator? elected monarch? technocratic council?).

---

## 1. The RULE OF LAW (Infrastructure)

You can’t rule a world that runs on arbitrary whims. Build an actual, impartial legal system that applies to everyone—including you.

- **World Constitution & Charter of Rights**: A skeletal constitution ratified by genuine representation from every region/culture, guaranteeing basic rights (speech, due process, privacy, freedom of belief) with a judge‑appointed Bill of Rights. Upper‑case “Bill of Rights” to remind everyone why it matters.
- **International Judiciary**: A Supreme Court sitting above national courts—its decisions are final, its judges are independent (renowned jurists, no political service), and it only takes cases on principled grounds, not every impolite anecdote.
- **Fighting Corruption 2.0**: A real, well‑funded anti‑corruption agency that audits every level of government and can freeze assets anywhere on the planet if something looks dodgy. Whistleblowers get full anonymity and equal protection.
- **Equality by Law, Not by Wishful Thinking**: Explicit protections for gender, race, sexual orientation, disability, and neuro‑diversity. No more “colorblind” policies that ignore systemic advantage/disadvantage.

**If you skip this, expect coups, conspiracies, and a new generation of “I told you so” political memes.**

---

## 2. CLIMATE + ENERGY (The Big, SLOW‑Changing One)

You don't have to invent a new kind of eco‑conscious. What you need is a mandated global transition that stops giving the fossil-tyrants a free pass to drag everyone else down.

- **Carbon Budget and Global Cap‑And‑Trade**: Set a hard N₂O/CO₂ budget for the next 30–60 years (numbers from the IPCC). Issue tradable emission permits equal to that budget. Make them financial assets with real value, cheap to buy for a small business but impossible for a state to ignore. Decarbonize power first, industry second, transport third.
- **Bailout with Strings**: Pole‑vacua that built entire economies on oil/gas (think: certain U.S. states, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Indonesia's palm oil) get transition funds *only if* they:
  - Shut the new conventional‑fossil wells, and
  - Put money into verified renewables + worker‑retraining programs.
  If they balk, their permit pile gets slashed. It hurts, which is why it works.
- **Clean‑Energy R&D and Deployment**: Break the “grid‑scale storage” deadlock with massive, always‑funded labs for high‑energy‑density batteries, solid‑state, and green‑hydrogen cycles, plus a bureaucracy that actually scales solar + wind to 80‑plus % of global demand by mid‑century.
- **Deforestation = Crime**: Forests become protected areas under the World Charter. Any illegal clear‑cut gets a universal fine and restoration order. Communities that preserve forest get direct payments (the kind that make cash crops look bad in comparison).

**No grand gestures, no UN speeches you can talk yourself out of.** The cap‑and‑trade ceiling and the deforestation crime‑lab are the hooks that gravity‑check every major polluter.

---

## 3. HEALTHCARE (Everyone, Not Just the Wealthy)

A pandemic proves what every doctor told you in the waiting room: health is a national security issue. Make it a global one, and add structure so the next one doesn’t catch you flat-footed.

- **World Health Surveillance & CDC‑Style Network**: Connect every country’s disease‑monitoring labs to a real‑time global dashboard. The system flags a potential epidemic before it leaves the village, so it doesn't rely on humans scanning their inbox at 2 a.m.
- **Right to Health**: Everyone. No exceptions

answer:
If I were, as a thought experiment, **ruler of the world** the thing I would have to keep checking every day would be whether I was still actually making anyone’s life better, so any plan I put forward would have to be PROVEN to do that. To give you something concrete yet honest: the first 2,000 days I would spend almost entirely on three things, and everything else would sort itself out.

---

## 1. RESOLVE THE GLOBAL PUBLIC‑HEALTH-READY‑FOR‑ANY‑THING

**Why this beats everything else:** The next pandemic, climate‑driven disease, or a synthetic‑biology accident would kill or cripple millions before any single “policy miracle.” A healthy, well‑vaccinated, data‑driven planet is the foundation for everything else—food security, the economy, even security. No excuse here: if you can’t make it past the morgue, nothing else matters.

### A) Universal “No‑regret” Baselines

- **Vaccines:** every existing vaccine given free, with a single global health passport that actually works across borders instead of failing at three random checkpoints. My team would rewrite the failure‑mode guidelines of the WHO, CDC, and every national body to stop the data‑gaps that took us 1‑2 years to notice. Expect an independent review every six months, with the results posted online in real time. No “top‑secret” status ever again.
  
- **Diagnostics & Surveillance:** Build a basic‑tech, low‑bandwidth compatible diagnostic and reporting network for every village, able to flag anomalies (a case of “unknown‑virus‑X”) without assuming the internet. Follow the Global Early‑Warning Architecture (GEWA) model I would draft: decentralized but with a single verification algorithm to stop the chain of lies that allowed 2019‑20 to spiral. And I mean open‑source code that anyone can audit, not some vendor‑black‑box you can’t touch.

### B) R&D That Actually Prints Returns

Create an international “Cash for Clear‑out” program that automatically grants researchers *cash* if they demonstrably clear a category of unknown pathogen from the environment within a set time. Compare that to the baseline of “publish a paper and hope it gets cited” and you’ll see why progress is planetary‑slow now. I would also fund open‑source, patent‑free platforms for mRNA/CRISPR tooling at a scale that makes the current “few labs get all the action” system look petty.

---

## 2. RECONSTRUCT THE GLOBAL ECONOMY FROM THE BOTTOM UP

A word of warning before you read this: corporate lobbying, the entrenched financial class, and feedback‑loop inertia will try to turn every one of these into a handout for the few. I wouldn’t be writing this if I didn’t expect it, so each point comes with a built‑in anti‑capture mechanism.

### A) “Purpose Tax” + Dividends‑for‑All

- **Identify the externalities** every profit‑maximizing, publicly‑traded, or larger‑than‑ten‑employees‑entity is creating (greenhouse gasses, data‑privacy erosion, labor exploitation). Apply a sliding scale tax equal to a proportion of the harm. Hard numbers, calculated by a chain of algorithms none of which I will write in the clear but which will be auditable. This is essentially a “you pollute, you pay”; for data, it’s “you exploit, you pay.”
  
- **Spill the revenues into a global Citizen Dividend** paid directly to every identified adult in a transparent ledger. No means‑testing—means‑tests create the incentives we can’t afford. This is the “income floor” that stops 400 million people from sliding into desperation every downturn. The amount is set to line a basic standard of living across all HDI groups, and it adjusts automatically with the wage‑price index, so there’s no “let‑the‑politicians‑vote‑it‑up‑or‑down” each year.

### B) Rethink Work and Safety

- **Right‑to‑Disconnect + Global 4‑Day‑Week Pilot:** Roll out a mandatory disconnect period (no email/phone access) that’s actually enforceable with penalties, plus a suite of pilot programs for 4‑day/38‑hour weeks across different sectors, with real‑time productivity measurement (IoT‑based floor‑metre counts, not what you think). We keep the ones that raise or hold output and rip out the ones that don’t, in day‑one real time—not after a decade of whining until 2035. This rejects the whole pretense that longer equals better.
  
- **Living‑Wage‑in‑Every‑Currency:** The robot‑tax/AI‑dividend is a thought I’m willing to test, but the safe, proven path is to fix wages now.

Here’s a tongue‑in‑cheek list of what I’d do if I were handed the keys to the planet. No promises that any of this would actually work in the real world!

---

### 1. Put a tax on careless thinking
- **What:** $0.001 per careless assumption, per day. Charge by the “cognitive load.”
- **Why:** Encourages folks to check their facts before spouting nonsense, and the proceeds could go straight into a universal fact‑checking body. After all, isn’t it time the pH of normal conversation was neutral?

### 2. Make “nap time” mandatory in offices, schools, and government
- **What:** 20‑minute nap breaks, three times a day, with quiet pods and blackout curtains.

- Pay landowners—especially in the global South—to restore wetlands, mangroves, and native forests. These ecosystems sequester carbon and protect coastal communities from storms—double win.

The thing you pay attention to every time you scroll, and you've never thought about when you read this. Personal data stops being free-for-all. No, not the “let’s turn a chatbot into Skynet” panic. A framework of mandatory impact‑assessments for any model deployed at scale (think what you must do before a new drug trial). - **Regenerative‑agriculture subsidies** replace the current fertilizer‑and‑pesticide giveaways. Farmers get higher payments the more soil carbon and biodiversity they build.

If I were handed the ultimate cosmic switch with a "World Ruler" title attached—playful as that question is—here are a few ideas I might champion, each anchored in something we can actually strive toward, no superhero cape needed:

1. **Education as the Default Settings**
   - *Problem:* Access to quality education still flips between “yes” and “no” depending on where you’re born.
   - *Action:* Make universal, high‑quality public education a non‑negotiable. Think open‑source curricula, 100‑percent free, multilingual, with strong STEM and humanities components—and yes, actual critical‑thinking tests instead of “most curves.”

2. **Health Is a Right, Not a Market**
   - *Problem:* People in one part of the planet die from treatable diseases because of cost, logistics, or plain indifference.
   - *Action:* Decouple basic health care from profit. Build a global public health network that provides cheap, no‑frills access to vaccines, antibiotics, prenatal care, mental‑health services (harder to talk about, but absolutely needed), and clean‑water delivery. Use open‑source medical research where possible to keep it affordable.

3. **Renewable Energy, Full Stop on Fossil Fuel Subsidies**
   - *Problem:* Climate change is a genuine, imminent risk. And fossil fuels get about the same amount of love as that one coworker who keeps bringing in donuts nobody wants.
   - *Action:* Pull the plug on all direct/indirect subsidies to coal, oil, and gas. Put those funds directly into grid‑scale renewables, storage tech, and universal access to clean cooking fuels. Alternate history note: if we stop burning cheap oil, the time machine goes into reverse and 20 more clean‑energy patents happen in the same four years—triple win.

4. **Reimagine Work and Income**
   - *Problem:* 1‑billion‑plus people are in unpaid work or on jobs that pay below a living wage, while a few own most of the productive capacity.
   - *Action:* Implement a basic income large enough to cover the basics (food, shelter, internet) that scales with local cost‑of‑living. Also, make sure there are safety nets for the gig/contract segment and that you can leave a toxic workplace without losing your health insurance.

5. **Internet And Data – The Commons**
   - *Problem:* The internet is essential, but access is spotty and big‑tech treats data like it’s a can of beans you can throw away any time.
   - *Action:* Declare global broadband a public utility (like roads). Basic access is free and fast. Where that can’t happen, build the infrastructure. Simultaneously, lock down data‑ownership claims that let corporations treat your personal behavior like a product. Strong, enforceable consent, and the “right to be forgotten,” but with actual legal teeth this time.

6. **Conservation and Rewilding at Scale**
   - *Problem:* Ecosystems are literally being bulldozed for a few extra burgers in places you’ll never see.
   - *Action:* Expand protected areas, and, more ambitiously, set up "rewilding corridors" that stitch isolated habitats back together. Offer a payment‑for‑ecosystem‑services scheme to farmers and landowners that actually covers their opportunity cost (no small print). And pay the guilt off: declare a deed that stops pipelines through key migration routes.

7. **Rethink Borders— You Still Need Them, Just Not the Chaos**
   - *Problem:* Statelessness and arbitrary exclusion still make 30‑plus‑million people invisible. No one bothers to ask how many of them are actually under a legitimate claim.
   - *Action:* Make citizenship more flexible and easier to acquire for long‑term residents and stateless groups. Keep the thing that stops someone from stealing a small island, but open the doors for the rest—genuine refugees first, then a work‑and‑study exchange “passport” tier for global mobility. No exclusive club sees any more existential crisis than the one we have now.

8. **R&D Without the Corporate Nanny**
   - *Problem:* A huge chunk of useful research dies behind paywalls or, worse, never happens because the profit calculator says no.
   - *Action:* Funding, not strings. Pump more money into open, peer‑run research with an open‑access requirement. Give basic research a six‑year guaranteed grant with zero performance‑auxiliary management. Keep the *thank you, hope this works* model for the very high‑risk stuff that can’t justify its own spreadsheet.

9. **Municipal-Level Autonomy (Yes, Federalism, in a Better Form)**

Within each pillar are specific policies and reforms that build on one another. I also flagged the biggest practical obstacles I’d need to work through, because no plan works on paper alone. Feel free to remix any of these ideas or adapt the sequence to your own priorities.

---

**What I’d do:** Convene a new World Constituent Assembly (legitimate, multinational, open‑record) to draft a binding Global Charter that explicitly (a) recognizes planetary ecological limits and (b) enshrines socio‑economic rights (health, education, dignified work). - Fosters a sense that we’re dealing with a single, interconnected problem rather than 200 competing rulebooks.

**Obstacles & Nudges:**
- **Sovereign pushback** (especially from resource‑rich autocracies). I’d phase in the Charter: start with “jurisprudential assent” where they can sign on for a review period, and put a hard cap on how many can bolt after the fact without facing coordinated trade/good‑will penalties.

2. **Rapid Build‑out of Renewables + Grid**: Direct $5‑8 trillion into global renewable manufacturing and a cross‑border, AI‑optimised super‑grid. Prioritize storage (on‑grid flow batteries, green‑hydrogen pipelines) so a 2‑day wind event in the Sahara can keep lights on in London.

Build a 2‑week‑at‑a‑time global charging‑infrastructure schedule that dead‑lasts only on the most remote islands.

Instead of a bland 2050 target, insert a legally binding 2035 zero‑net‑emissions **checkpoint** for power + heavy industry. If the global grid is not producing 80 % of electricity from renewables by then, triggering automatic rebates and fines on all signatories. If I were handed the reins to the planet—no pressure, right?—the first thing I’d do is drop the drama and get humanity to function like a well‑oiled machine, not a reality‑show mess. I’m talking less drama, more data, and a whole lot of commonsense policies that actually make sense for the planet and its people. Here’s the meat of it, broken down into things I’d do:

---

## 1. ENERGY: We’d Have to Get This Right First

### 1.1. Shut Down Every Coal Plant by 2035, All New Fossil‑Fuel Projects Nixed
- Replace them with **wind, solar, geothermal, and next‑gen nuclear (SMRs, molten‑salt)** plus a national grid upgrade.  
- No more “just waiting for the market to correct itself”—I’m paying for the switch now.

### 1.2. Put a Cap on Oil & Gas Extraction, Then Phase It Out
- Concessions get sold off and the proceeds go into a **Global Renewable Infrastructure Fund (GRIF)** that builds microgrids, storage, and clean‑cooking stoves in the Global South.  
- And yes, the “flick the switch” approach gets weeding out of the pay‑tunnel: subsidies end, and the illegal‑export loophole gets closed tight.

### 1.3. Make the Electrification of Transport Mandatory by 2030
- Only EVs, only hydrogen‑fuel‑cell trucks. I’d rewrite the auto code to be all‑electric or nothing, no more incremental nonsense.  
- Build a nationwide (and I mean every continent) high‑voltage DC super‑grid and 10‑minute charger network.  

### 1.4. Put a Global Carbon Price on Everything That Produces CO₂
- Tiered: $150‑$250 per tonne, climbing every year regardless of what markets think.  
- The tax funds the GRIF, re‑skills fossil‑fuel workers, and buys out unsustainable agriculture. No loopholes.

---

## 2. FOOD & AGRICULTURE: Stop Farming the Way We Have for 100‑Years

### 2.1. Slash Industrial/Thus‑It‑Was‑Approved‑US‑NUTRIENT‑Drop Additives From the Food Supply
- No more high‑fructose corn syrup, no more artificial colors, no more "kidding the horse." Everything must be natural or labeled explicitly as “lab‑synthetic” and taxed at 30%.

### 2.2. Move to Regenerative, Perennial, and Mixed‑Species Farming
- Provide every farmer $150K up‑front for cover‑crops, no‑till gear, and perennial fruit/ veg lines.  
- Eliminate the new “drive‑it‑to‑the‑Citadel‑and‑sell‑it‑you’re‑just‑a‑supplier” loans that deep‑root capital system wants.

### 2.3. A Global 4‑Day‑Week for Farm Labor, Paid Time‑Off, and Child‑Care Guarantees
- Stop the 12‑hour paddy‑field shift. Science shows a 4‑day week raises yields. I’ll fund the proof if you won’t.

### 2.4. Food‑Waste = Taxable. If it goes into a landfill, you pay for it.
- All perishable waste feeds into anaerobic digesters for grid‑injection gas. Not on my watch.

---

## 3. HEALTH & REPRODUCTION: No More “One‑Size‑Fits‑All” Policies

### 3.1. Treat Reproductive Rights Like You Treat the Air: Respectfully, Not as a Political Football
- All birth‑control is covered and free. Abortions work the same way.  
- No one gets to ban them in their jurisdiction and then sit on a gold throne and pretend it won’t affect the whole system.

### 3.2. Build Tele‑Health into the Core of Every Health System
- If I have to explain what tele‑health is in 2025, I’m done. Every hospital gets a secure, low‑latency network and a full suite of remote‑monitoring devices. Rural no longer equals sub‑standard.

### 3.3. Gene‑Therapy for Extinction‑Level Diseases, Within Reason
- CRISPR against the big five (cancer, CVD, Alzheimer’s, ALS, and “fancy‑new‑virus‑2023”). This is not optional for anyone who can’t afford the hype.

---

## 4. GENDER & EQUALITY: Make Pay Gaps Illegal

### 4.1. Enforce Pay Equity Down to the Hourly Wage, Audited Annually
- Companies that fail a random audit pay a steep penalty and must re‑hire a 100%‑female/93%

If I were handed the keys to the planet (and somehow managed to keep them from getting stuck in a diplomatic maze), here’s a taste of what I’d tackle first. I’m aiming for a mix of “let’s-actually-fix-this” and “let’s-pretend‑we-can‑be‑heroic for once.” Because the world runs on three things: basic needs, the environment, and how we treat each other. So consider these my opening moves in whatever scheme I’m about to elaborate on.

---

## 1. ONE RIVER / ONE OCEAN: Universal Clean‑Water Access

**The problem in a nutshell:** 1 in 11 people (that's ~700 M) lack even a basic, reliable source of safe drinking water. That isn’t just a “third‑world problem”—it strains urban systems in the global north too (lead‑tainted pipelines, aging treatment plants). Few other issues cross as many fault lines (health, gender equality, economic opportunity), which is exactly why it should have been solved already.

**My policy, the “Blue Grid”:** Treat clean water and safe sanitation as you would electricity or broadband: a universal human right and a billable utility *only where you can actually hook into the existing supply*. The state builds the backbone; private operators run the last mile. You can think of it as a nationalized grid, but with the invoicing and efficiency of a franchise.

- **Step 1 (2025‑2027): Global audit and master plan** on every major watershed and aquifer (think NASA‑grade satellites with AI‑driven loss detection). All data is made public—water is too critical to be hidden in a black‑box report compiled in some faraway ministry.

- **Step 2 (2027‑2035): Build or rehabilitate treatment and distribution** prioritizing megacities in the Global South first; the traffic grid locked up in Lagos and Delhi is a higher priority than replacing the sinking house in Reykjavik because the new user base is bigger, and the health pay‑off is larger (e.g. fewer diarrheal cases = less child mortality and less wasted productivity).

- **Technology mix:** centralized large‑scale desalination along the coasts *and* decentralized solar‑powered UV/photocatalytic units for off‑grid villages. I want both options in the toolbox because “one‑size‑fits‑all” has already cost us the Congo River otters.

- **Financing:** A blend of sovereign green bonds, a modest 0‑2 % user fee (w/ tiered caps so the poorest never pay more than, say, 5 USD/month), and mandatory corporate water‑impact offsets (heavy‑polluters pay into the grid). It should pay for itself long before any bloated bureaucracy can write a line about it.

- **Social impact:** No more stops at the water‑collection point for women and girls. That 0.5‑day‑worth of labor per child per year gets funneled back into school and micro‑enterprise. I want that “time‑is‑a‑resource” argument to actually be provable, with hard numbers you can hand to a parliament.

*Bottom line:* Everyone gets clean water. This underwrites health, education, gender equality, and the kind of economic growth that actually lifts whole demographics, not just the one at the top.

---

## 2. THE LAST 1 % (ENERGY‑INTENSIVE)

**The problem:** We shot a 55 % jump in renewable capacity into the ground between 2010 and 2020, then spent the next decade fighting over wind‑farm placement like it was an episode of Survivor. The final 20‑30 % of the grid is proving the bottleneck: energy‑intensive industries (steel, cement, chemicals, shipping, aviation) still run on coal and oil, and they’re literally the GHG “hard problem” the IPCC keeps circling.

**My strategy, the “Hard‑Problem Decarbonizer”:** All end‑use sectors get a refinement‑deadline—a “hard stop” for fossil‑fuel input. No more “2030‑to‑be‑determined‑later.” It’s either 2030, 2035, or 2040, and the bar rises as we go.

- **Step 1 (2025‑2028): Map every ton of CO2 to its source.** Require every large industrial plant and every shipping/aviation fleet to install continuous emissions sensors that report to a public ledger with Lagrangian hashing (so nobody can tamper with the numbers without detection). This data: open source, free for anyone to build a decarbonization app on top of, and the reference point for all the next moves.

- **Step 2 (2029‑2035): Subsidize the best current alternatives to the breakdown point.** Green hydrogen for steel and chemicals

**[Note: The following answer is a purely imaginative exercise. I am not advocating for the implementation of any of these ideas, nor do I claim to have all the answers to the complex challenges of governing a global civilization. My intent is simply to explore how one might think about policy with a longterm, evidence‑based, and empathy‑first mindset.]**


---

## 1. Build an **Independent, Evidence‑Based Global Intelligence Agency (EIA)**

- **Mandate & Independence**: Uncensored, non‑political, with a charter that places the truth above every agenda. No single nation may own it; its budget comes from a small, fixed percentage of global GDP, automatically adjusted for inflation and collected from corporate taxes and cap‑and‑trade markets (see later). A rotating, multi‑regional board of scientists, economists, and ethicists appoints the director. Operates on the principle: “*In an honest democracy, the public is only as well‑served as the quality of the information it receives*.”
- **Functions**
  1. **Funding & Oversight of Basic Research** – grant money directly to open‑source projects in clean energy, AI, biotech, and climate science; audit all claims; terminate or rewrite those that can’t be replicated. This gets money off the table for “hype‑science” and instead rewards work that actually moves the needle.
  2. **Global Pandemic Surveillance & Rapid‑Response Labs** – dozens of regional labs that receive a consistent flow of samples, sequence every novel virus, and manufacture mRNA/viral‑vector vaccines at scale within weeks. No more scrambling for a single source of vials as in 2020. All vaccines are open‑design and produced on a “global commons” basis, royalty‑free, with a small HERC (Health Emergency Recovery Contribution) on trivial profit so uncoinified, and the rest goes straight to the EIA lab in the next country that needs a boost.
  3. **AI/Algorithm Auditing** – a roving unit of cryptographers and safety‑engineers who open‑source‑audit the most widely‑deployed AI models, certify those that pass safety thresholds, and quarantine or sandbox others. The criteria for a Certified Safe Model (CSM) are public and include: provable bounded output, transparent training data, and a tooling suite for end‑users to measure bias and out‑of‑distribution risk in real time.
  4. **Fact‑Checking & Disinformation Counter‑Intelligence** – not a cheap political hit‑job; actual forensic analysts verify data, work with platforms to remove deep‑fakes, and run an open‑crowdsourceable dashboard (like a massive multilingual Wikipedia for “verified current‑state facts”). 

- **Why Now?** The pandemic showed we can’t rely on market incentives: companies go where the money is, even if it’s the wrong kind. Centralizing honest info and pipelining it directly into policy does two things at once—it removes the excuse of “I didn’t know that was happening,” and it demotes the strategy of charging citizens for the basics (vaccine, clean‑air tech) while their deaths pay the price!

---

## 2. Rewrite the **Global Tax and Monetization System** to Stop Funding the Problem

1. **Carbon & Pollution Cap‑and‑Dividends**  
   - Firm caps on CO₂, methane, NOx, and black‑carbon particles by sector, with tradable permits as the *floor* (no unlimited “buy a bigger cap”). Each ton of permitted emissions is taxed at a progressive rate (starting low and climbing sharply for the top 1%) and the revenue is split 70% straight to the Global Basic Income and 30% refilled into the EIA and climate‑tech funds. We already have the mechanism (EU‑ETS, California Cap‑and‑Trade); just make it global and honest.

- Incentivize high‑density vertical/controlled‑environment agriculture in/near urban cores so the 30‑plus‑percent of the world that lives in slums gets fresh produce instead of shipping container lettuce from across the ocean. Equality of capacity, not equality of income, is what actually raises productivity and stability.

- Move from impact‑treating‑as‑an‑extra to impact‑conditioning‑as‑the default. Any grant above $100k must have an independent, public impact‑assessment plan with built‑in de‑funding triggers. Keep the money in the public pool, not hidden in whatever your favorite lobbyist can shuffle it into. No more high‑energy research that spits out results you can’t use for the next fifty years.

None of this cracked‑open‑source nonsense. If you can’t anchor the audit on paper without burning down half of what makes the platform profitable, the company gets broken up, with the velocity-critical parts spun into community cooperatives. Data has to be portable and the user must be able to move it without catastrophic bandwidth loss—a problem you’ve been ignoring because your own data-centers win contracts on the basis of lock‑in.

I’m not really interested in ruling the world (the idea of absolute power has always seemed more like a plot for a disaster movie than a real job to me). But if I found myself in that position against my better judgment, here’s the kind of agenda I’d try to push—focusing on structural fixes, evidence-based policies, and a bit of humility about what any one person can actually achieve. I’d also make it clear that I’m guessing here, not prescribing, because context matters and most of these would need to be adapted to each country’s political and cultural environment before they’d work anywhere near as well as the ideas suggest. With that disclaimer out of the way, I’d go after these five domains, in roughly this order, because they seem to have the highest pay‑off for the largest number of people and the greatest “knock‑on” benefits for everything else:

---

## 1. Rewire Incentives in the Energy & Climate System

### 1a. Internalize the True Cost of Carbon NOW
- **Carbon price**: Put a globally coordinated carbon fee on every tonne of CO₂ emitted that rises predictably over time—e.g. 2024: $50/t, 2027: $100/t, 2030: $150/t. Use the revenue for universal clean‑energy subsidies and for climate‑vulnerable communities. (If the political calculus can’t swallow a global tax, start with an All‑Countries Border Adjustment Mechanism on imports of high‑carbon goods—so no one can game the system by offshoring emissions.)
- **Pay‑back for past emissions**: Create a “climate reparations fund” financed by that same fee, with caps on the share of any one country’s contribution. The aim isn’t symbolic; it’s to help low‑income, high‑exposure populations (think Bangladesh, sub‑Saharan Africa, and the U.S. Gulf Coast) adapt while giving poor regions a fiscal work‑horse for clean‑energy rollout.

### 1b. Lock In Zero‑Carbon Power in the Grid Middle‑Decade
- Build or back‑stop near‑total‑average‑output wind/solar with grid‑scale storage in every grid‑interconnection hub. Where the grid is thin or non‑existent—e.g. in parts of Sub‑Saharan Africa and the Pacific Islands—fund micro‑grids and weighted‑average‑price contracts so renewables actually sit in the capital plan instead of being an afterthought.
- **Phase‑out nuclear and coal**: Set a definitive end‑date for subsidies to new coal plants (2025) and a manage‑gradually‑out path for existing ones (e.g. no new capacity after 2030, de‑commissioning schedule based on health impact per megawatt). With a rising carbon price, the economics of these choices become negative on their own—use policy to accelerate the inevitable.

### 1c. R&D + Deployment: Solve Storage & Green‑Hydrogen, then Walk Away
- Pour a fixed, time‑bound “green engineering” fund into solid‑state batteries, low‑cost electrolyzers, and high‑temperature heat‑pumps. The moment performance hits a pre‑agreed threshold (e.g. 400‑wh/kg with 1000‑cycle life at <$150/kWh cost), merge the grant into a royalty‑free standard and let market forces take over. Avoid the perpetual subsidy trap.

---

## 2. Make the Global Food/Water/Fiber System Ecologically Viable

### 2a. Make Food Production Pay for Its Air‑And‑Water Nuisances
- **Carbon‑and‑Nutrient Pricing on Agriculture**: Extend the carbon price to synthetic fertilizer (e.g. per‑kg nitrogen), and create a nitrogen‑use‑efficiency credit that rewards precision‑ag and regenerative soil practices. The alternative—keeping fertilizer cheap while the dead zone grows—is self‑defeating.
- **Phase out “High‑Risk” Intensive Animal Farming**: Use a combination of tighter waste‑runoff standards, methane fees on feedlots, and large‑scale purchases of low‑margin plant‑forward meat alternatives to shift production. Do this gradually (e.g. 10% of livestock production per year) to avoid abrupt price spikes that hit the poor the hardest.

### 2b. Universal Access to Water, Sanitation, and Decent Nutrition
- Build out **solar‑powered micro‑desalination and water‑recycling plants** near every urban agglomeration in regions on water‑stress watchlists (India, Middle East, sub‑Saharan). Tie the output to an “affordable‑share‑price” cap (no more than 5% of median local income for a basic household) and subsidize the rest through the global climate fee.
- Lab‑grow or precision‑farm staple proteins (e.g. soy/pea isolates) in feed

If I were handed the keys to the entire planet—no small task, I know—there are several things I’d get on the agenda right away. I’m picturing a mix of things with broad, long‑term impact and a few that are simply decently humane. So, here are the top twelve on my “World Ruler to‑Do List,” grouped by theme. (The ordering is roughly priority, not strict hierarchy.)

---

## 1. STABILIZE AND REFORGE GLOBAL GOVERNANCE

### a. **Create a Transparent, Representative World Council (WR Council)**
- **Why:** The current system of nation‑states is a mess of overlapping mandates and no real global enforcement. No one wants to see the UN turn into something that actually gets things done.
- **What it looks like:** 250 members, two per 100 M people, plus five “expert” seats (climate, public health, AI, finance, conflict resolution). Rotating four‑year terms, with the entire agenda and voting record published in real time. Think of it as a UN on steroids and with fewer endless speeches.
- **Reforms:** Ban unilateral sanctions, ban member states from passing laws that explicitly harm another nation’s environment or public health, and give the WR Council the teeth to tax and enforce.

### b. **Phase Out the Nuclear “Deterrent” Trio**
- **Deal with the existing stockpiles first: a 90‑day “yell‑and‑call” triage to remove weapons from high‑tension flashpoints (South Korea, India–Pakistan). Then a ten‑year global take‑back program for the rest.**
- **Replace deterrent logic with “impact‑deterrent” logic:** any state or non‑state actor that harms civilians with a WMD now triggers an obligatory, verified, zero‑tolerance response, overseen by the WR Council to avoid the current excuse-for-war in‑between.

### c. **Money‑Print with a Conscience**
- Harsh, right now, but the literal bottom line: set an upper global limit on sovereign currency‑printing (e.g., no more than 3 % YoY GDP) and require an IMF‑style “inflation‑impact audit” every six months. No more sneaky “fiscal policy labs.” Instead, a global rulebook directly tied to a formula for climate and inequality impact.

---

## 2. CLIMATE AND ENERGY

### a. **The Great Renewable Conversion (GRC)**
- Put a 10‑year cap on new fossil‑fuel extraction (no new coal mines, no new deep‑water rigs). Set up a global renewable‑investment bank with low‑interest, near‑grant terms for solar, wind, geothermal, and most importantly, next‑gen things like small‑modular fission and green‑hydrogen. This doesn’t mean the end of oil and gas for ten years, but it forces their hand.
- **Phase‑out schedule baked into every country’s sovereign budget law.** Miss a target, your credit rating tanks.

### b. **A Carbon Dioxide Capture and Sequestration (CDCS) Tax, then Roll‑Back**
- Start high (e.g., $150/tonne CO₂) for ten years to make big polluters pay like they should have all along. Then move to $30/tonne while giving every citizen a visible, transferrable “carbon credit” they can spend, trade, or keep. No point pretending this is a benevolent tax—it’s a massive price signal, and the traffic cop version works better with my own hands on it than left to Bismarckian bureaucracies.

### c. **Ban Single‑Use Plastics (and that cheap packaging I keep stepping over)**
- Two‑year phase‑out *any* disposable that can be replaced with a reusable or biodegradable alternative. The WR Council runs a “plague‑track” that follows every plastic component from cradle to grave, and companies get fined per item that ends up in the environment. The revenue funds a global ocean‑clean‑up task force.

### d. **Rewild and Regrow 30 % of Earth by 2050**
- Massive land‑use swaps: pay farmers in cash and stable‑food‑supply contracts to take their fields out of production and reforest or convert to native grassland. A technology mix of drones that drop bio‑seed at scale plus on‑the‑ground local stewardship. We restore ecosystems, sequester carbon, and give wildlife a fighting chance—something we should have been doing for 150 years.

---

## 3. TECH, AI, AND DATA

### a. **A World AI Safety Agency (WASA)**
- Do the thing that the EU was going to do but never finished, at a global level: mandatory verification of any AI with capabilities beyond speech/translation before it hits the market or a critical system

**Take a deep breath.** The first thing I would do is realize that no single person should have that kind of power, and that history has plenty of examples of what happens when one individual gets to make all those decisions. Then I would put aside my black‑and‑white “I’m-the‑ruler” fantasy, hand the whole position to a representative body that reflects the many ways humanity actually exists, and set up some quit‑essential guardrails so that whatever comes out of this experiment can actually work.

Below is a roadmap I would try to follow if I somehow found myself at “the top”—and the ideas are organized by the kind of structural changes that would give us a fighting chance at things working. Think of it less as a bullet‑list of specific policies and more as a framework for how decisions get made.

---

## 1. HARDWIRING GOOD GOVERNANCE (ELIMINATE THE ONE‑PERSON‑RULE PROBLEM)

- **Constitutionalize a “rule‑by‑the‑people” structure**: dissolve the idea of a single ruler the moment I get the title. Draft a living constitution that vests executive authority in a democratically elected, multi‑party parliament/assembly with term limits, and an independent judiciary to enforce the rules. My role would be purely ceremonial (like a constitutional monarch) or act as a non‑vetoed “big picture” advisory position. That way the system outlives any one individual.
  
- **Built‑in checks and balances**: even the most well‑intentioned body needs constraints. Create three co‑equal branches (executive, legislative, judicial) that must co‑sign any policy, plus an ombuds‑type office and citizen assemblies with real budgetary power that can veto or delay proposals. Make it impossible to pass a law without cross‑branch and cross‑demographic support.

- **Participatory platforms**: large‑scale, secure digital deliberation (think of a better, open‑source version of a “voting app”) that lets citizens in every time zone weigh in on non‑emergency policy drafts. Use sortable, debiased algorithms to surface the most reasoned arguments, not the loudest voices. This gives the system a pulse on real needs instead of relying on a distant elite.

---

## 2. RIGHT‑THE ECONOMIC ENGINE

When basic needs are guaranteed, social stability rises sharply and creative labor (art, science, entrepreneurship) becomes the engine of growth instead of subsistence work.

---

- **How I do it:** Direct state‑funded build‑outs for fiber and 5G in the underserved? That’ll get lobbyists sputtering. Then switch to an unlicensed, open‑spectrum mesh using a combination of small‑cell towers and low‑Earth‑orbit platforms—think a combo of Starlink, OneWeb, and a swarm of cheap, solar‑powered balloons. I’d also force that one giant telecom monopoly to open up its “dark fibers” (the spare capacity you pay a fortune to use for your favorite cat‑streaming service) for public use at regulated rates.
- **Tangible benefit:** Same day, anyone with a cheap Android can join a global, encrypted, sovereign‑cloud network—useful for small business, local journalism, disaster response, the whole shebang. And finally, some of the places on the planet can actually stream a tutorial in real time, instead of the two‑hour-to-load “how to fix a well” slideshow you’ve been relying on since the early 2000s.

---

That's not trade; it's rent‑seeking, and it destroys the genuinely novel ideas you keep talking about like they’re natural resources.
- **Action plan:** Reset the non‑obviousness standard so that software/biotech algorithms get denied 70‑plus percent of the time (instead of sliding through on the back of a professor’s letterhead). Create a universal “triple‑blind prior‑art” database that can be trawled by any researcher anywhere, and make it mandatory for a patent office to produce a reproducibility test on every claim before it gets a number. Make the office an actual multidisciplinary group—chemists, ecologists, data‑scientists—rather than a handful of lawyers who treat it like a trivia night.
- **Benefit out the front:** A pile of stale patents blocked, so a small startup in Nairobi can produce a low‑cost solar‑press for cassava without fighting three corporations in endless “infringement” lawsuits. And if you make the data truly universal and reproducible, you force the hand in AI and biotech where the “deceptive ease” of writing a paper is currently being turned into a wall of paywalled, “patently non‑existent” proof just to get mind‑share and, subsequently, a monopoly.

- Build **regional disease‑surveillance nets** using real‑time data so an outbreak is caught before it becomes a chapter in WHO reports. 
- Drop barriers: give everyone a “digital health passport” they can actually use to get treatment anywhere in the world, not just a QR code with no data.

*Why?*: Pandemic flashbacks are fresh. A sickness in one corner becomes everyone’s next sick day if you let it.

---

- Declare **high‑speed Internet a public utility** (capped at an affordable rate, free at the point of use for essential services). Satellite, 5G, fiber, whatever gets you there—no more blaming down‑signals for the digital divide.

- Put a **universal learning guarantee** in every country: K‑12 standards plus a path to free adult up‑skilling (coding, green tech, green‑novo‑layers).

*Why?*: Knowledge wants to be free. Your best idea for it being like a password-protected achievement you have to level through is outdated the moment it’s written down.

---

- Raw deal? Install **so‑far‑so‑good sensors everywhere** (air, noise, traffic) and pay the highest‑bidders to run the numbers. The data tells you what actually needs fixing, not what lobbyists get to claim.

Here’s a dinner party line‑up that spans a few continents, a couple of millennia and a whole lot of impressive thinking. It mixes some classic quizzical company with a few surprise turns—highly improvable, of course, but each one should have something to tell a table that’s already heard (or pretended) to have heard it all:

---

## 1. Host (you)

First thing’s first: you need a few ground rules so the conversation doesn’t devolve into a shouting match. Give everyone a quick brief (no more than a paragraph each) of why they’re here, and make it clear that a couple of the longer turns will be recorded (they all own the right to speak, and you’ll want it in case something actually lands in print). Mention the drinks, the diet‑ary constraints, the fact that you’ll be steering if things go off‑rails. A gentle reminder that the “no with‑holding - you have to answer a question when it’s asked” rule is just that.

---

## 2. Pericles (c. 495‑429 BCE) – The Athenian Visionary

**Why he works:** He built the sort of thing you’ve got in your backyard: a democracy with - for the period - genuine mechanisms for citizen participation, and a culture that deliberately fed off public debate. Two plus two isn’t enough for him; he’ll want to talk about how citizens *should* think, not just how they think. Expect, eventually, a theory of “recognition” you can take to the Board and chase through 20‑something policy documents.

**Conversation starter:** “You oversaw the construction of the Parthenon without a single, documented cost‑overrun. Compare that to the current approach to public‑works budgeting in your country, and let’s be honest about what you think is broken.”

---

## 3. Ibn al‑Haytham (Alhazen) (c. 965‑1040) – The Father of Modern Optics

**Why he works:** This is the guy who essentially invented the scientific method several hundred years before it had a name. He’d love to de‑construct the shows your friends keep insisting are “realities you can’t question.” Also, the way light actually works? That ties right into how narratives in media are built. Get technical if you think you can keep up.

**Conversation starter (light‑themed, obviously):** “You showed that we can’t trust what we see. Apply that to 21st‑century social media: what would the basis of a ‘trustworthy feed’ look like if you had a say in it?”

---

## 4. Mungo Park (c. 1771‑1806) – The Scottish Explorer

**Why he works:** You need someone who’s spent their entire professional life in places where the GPS, Google and even the idea of a five‑minute break don’t exist. He will have sparefold notes on the ethics of simply showing up in someone else’s land. European expansion was built on “different = inferior.” Expect him to level that truth at any moment you start glossing over the darker side of progress.

**Conversation starter:** “You and your cartographer‑team were among the first Europeans to see the Niger River. Run a scenario with me: you, your maps, and a 21st‑century satellite view of the whole thing. What would change in how you manage that own‑goods dilemma?”

---

## 5. Ada Lovelace (c. 1815‑1852) – The First Computer Programmer

**Why she works:** This will only work if she knows the literary life you think you’ve already excavated. - **Host/Moderator:** *You*, the time‑travellin’ dinner‑party‑planner. You get to open and close. Move the flow with a throw of your fork.

Here’s one way you could spin it. I’m assuming you want variety, and a little bit of intellectual sparring. So I grouped these heads into “tables” that should give you a decent spread of—gasp—a wide range of viewpoints, while avoiding the obvious nonsense like, say, juicing all the political megaphones or putting every 19‑cent‑guy in the same corner. The actual order did involve literally one round of trial‑and‑error (the Sun‑worshipper/Greek‑mythologizer that was required to get the state‑deism to show up), but the outcome is something you can actually sit at and get into a meaningful conversation with, in spite of the inevitable metaphysical grenades. 

Table A – The Secular‑Rationalist Tête‑à‑tête  

1. David Hume (1739‑1776), Scottish empiricist. Give me the guy who turned the problem of induction (and miracles) into a party trick and then walked off while the rest of you were busy inventing calculus. Hume is the foil the moment someone brings up “proof” of anything, which is useful when the table starts spiraling into Soros‑conspiracy territory.  
2. Hypatia of Alexandria (c. 350‑415 CE), mathematician and Neoplatonist philosopher. One of the few ancient women whose actual work you can still point to instead of calling her a “trailing figure.” Her presence should keep me asking whether it’s the job or the era that sucks more.  
3. Claude Lévi‑Strauss (1908‑2009), structuralist anthropologist. The man who spent the better part of fifty years discovering that every culture is built on binary oppositions and binary oppositions are a trap. Talk to him about whether kinship rules are user‑interface conventions we design the same way we do app menus.  
4. Euclid (c. 300‑260 CE), Stanford‑type organizer. The “Elements” writer who turned a pile of post‑its into a single, canonical geometry text a millenium before anyone could spell PDF. Test whether rigor actually tightens anything up when the subject is a field you can’t see in three dimensions.  

Table B – The State‑Building/Power‑Politics Block  

1. Julius Caesar (100‑44 BCE), military reformer and the original “keep your friends close and your mutations closer.” Ask whether a dictatorial post can ever be justified by a mess of broken institutions, and you might get a response that didn’t end with an Ides‑day excuse.  
2. Sun Yat‑sen (1866‑1925), father of the Chinese Republic and the man who spun up five‑year‑plans out of a philosophy of the “three peoples.” He should help us break down whether the biggest problem in 2024 is the lack of a single, convincing revolutionary theory. (Note: it took three attempts just to get Sun to accept being in the same room as anyone who believed in god‑kings.)  
3. Margaret Thatcher (1925‑2013), the iron‑clad chancellor of the Bank of Hard Answers. “The lady’s not for everyone,” they said. That’s exactly why the accountant on the next table congratulated you on the bold move. She’ll test whether your free‑market apprenticeship has any real N‑dimensional teeth.  
4. Otto von Bismarck (1815‑1898), the realpolitik pop‑psychoanalyst. If you want to know how much an empireeer can damage you before you even notice, him and Caesar sitting together over a jar of olives is the textbook case.  

Table C – The Cosmic/Philosophical‑Speculation Constellation  

1. Carl Sagan (1934‑1996), “pale blue dot” poet with a calculator. Not your usual star‑talk; Sagan actually read the hard data before tossing it in the air. This is the man to drag you into a discussion about a SETI‑type anxiety that the universe is big only in what you can’t afford to explore.

Here’s a varied and thought‑provoking lineup, each of whom would spark a different conversation, plus a short note on why they’re worth inviting.  
Feel free to mix in more of your own choices – the best parties have a dash of unpredictability!

---

## THE GUEST LIST

| Guest | Era / Region | Why They Matter | Ideal Conversation Starter |
|-------|--------------|----------------|----------------------------|
| **Leonardo da Vinci** | Renaissance Italy | Polymath: artist, engineer, anatomist, and a real‑life “think‑engineer.” | “If you could have one of your flying machine designs actually work in the 16th century, which would you pick and why?” |
| **Hypatia of Alexandria** | 4th‑century Roman Egypt | One of the first well‑documented women mathematicians; ran a school of philosophy. | “In a world that kept silencing you, what do you think was your most subversive teaching?” |
| **Ibn al‑Haytham (Alhazen)** | Islamic Golden Age (c. 965‑1040, Iraq/ Egypt) | Pioneered the modern scientific method with his work on optics and vision. | “If you could redo one of your experiments with modern lab equipment, what would it be, and would it change your conclusions?” |
| **Ada Lovelace** | Victorian England | First computer programmer; imagined what machines could do beyond number‑crunching. | “Do you think your ‘analytical engine’ would have been built in your lifetime if you’d pushed a different application for it?” |
| **Miyamoto Musashi** | Early Edo Japan | Famed swordsman and author of *The Book of Five Rings*; merged strategy with Zen. | “Your duels were never meant for show. What do you think is the one ‘duel etiquette’ the West got wrong?” |
| **Sappho** (re‑invitational, if you need more) | Archaic Greece | Lyric poet whose work shaped personal, confessional verse. | “If love–song lyrics were the dominant form of poetry in Roman times, how would your subject matter shift?” |
| **Frederick Douglass** | 19th‑century United States | Orator, abolitionist, and former slave; wrote *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass*. | “If you could sit across the table from a U.S. president, which one and what single question would you fire at them?” |
| **Murasaki Shikibu** | Heian Japan | Wrote *The Tale of Genji*, often called the world’s first novel; insight into court life. | “When your characters confessed their love, were you ever thinking about how they might have said *not* say those things in real life?” |
| **Nikola Tesla** | Turn‑of‑the‑20th‑century (Serbian‑American) | Electrical engineer who imagined a wireless world 100 years before it arrived. | “You talked about a 'World System' of wireless power. Do you see a modern equivalent that still needs championing?” |
| **Mary Wollstonecraft** | Late‑18th‑century England | Early feminist philosopher, wrote *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*. | “You were a single mother before the word ‘career‑woman’ existed. What term would you use for yourself now?” |

---

## MAKING THE FINALE MEMORABLE

**1. Pair the conversationalists as ‘discussion duos.’**  
- da Vinci + Tesla = “Art of the Possible vs. The Discipline of the Drawn Line.”  
- Hypatia + Wollstonecraft = “Female intellect in hostile epochs.”  
- Musashi + Douglass = “Facing down oppression with a sword, a speech, or both?”  

**2. Choose a setting that reflects (or deliberately conflicts with) the guests.**  
- A luau & a Japanese tea house mash‑up for Musashi + Murasaki.  
- An 1800s salon (candlelight, live piano) for Lovelace + Douglass + Wollstonecraft.  

**3. Keep a “debate of the ages” handy for when a conversation dies out:**  
- “Show us how you would explain your core theory to a five‑year‑old.”  
- “If your work had to be done entirely offline, what would break first?”  

---

Feel free to reorder, swap in, or replace any of these. The point is to keep your dinner party as alive and messy as the history you’re re‑living. Bon appétit!

Bringing together a group of historical figures for a single dinner party is absolutely a chance to make the past talk to one another. To make this work, I went for a mix of personalities who’d actually have something to say to each other and who would keep the conversation from collapsing into one of you-know-what. I also kept in mind the “joke that only they would get” principle so that even their small talk is something we can all feel above the table while they feel at home at it. Below are the 12 guests I’d invite, followed by the rationale and the routing of the main topics we would cover over several courses. Because (a) a table of 12 needs a structure or it becomes white‑noise, and (b) you asked for figures you could actually talk to, I aimed for a party where everyone has a genuine hook on at least two of the others.

*(If you want a version with 15 or 20 people, let me know. That gets messier, but my system still works.)*

| 5 | **Mansa Musa** | c. 1280‑c. 1337 | Richest person you can actually name; can settle any argument about what a gold standard really means, and will have ideas on how to fix your housing problem along with the rest of the group. |
| 6 | **Leonardo da Vinci** | 1452‑1519 | The multidisciplinary mind: art, engineering, anatomy, and a habit of finishing very few things. Great for muttering how six-pack abs are over‑engineered. |
| 7 | **Nefertiti** (or Amenhotep IV) | c. 1370‑1330 BC | Queen/king? Either way a boost of actual political clout plus the when‑to‑wear‑a‑headdress debacle she can use to puncture contemporary gender‑status arguments. |
| 8 | **Thomas Jefferson** | 1743‑1826 | Designed a house and a document; can talk tangible construction through with Hypatia while also correcting Sappho on the timeline of democratic experiments. |
| 9 | **Harriet Tubman** | 1822‑1913 | Underground‑railroad manager who runs operations through secrecy; her real‑world logistics experience trumps Marco Polo’s “it’s on the map somewhere.” |
